author_final_remarks.value:
Dear AC, SAC, and Reviewers,

We sincerely thank the reviewers for their thorough and insightful reviews. Their recognition of the benchmark’s thoughtful construction, scale, richness, and comprehensive evaluation motivates us deeply. We are particularly encouraged by the positive feedback on the novel pairing of infographic and plain charts, the inclusion of visual-element and metaphor-based questions, and the rigorous analysis of MLLM performance gaps.

We have thoroughly addressed the reviewers' concerns through clarifications, benchmark enhancements, and additional experiments. The reviewers have acknowledged our revisions positively. For example, Vcyr noted, "I believe they have provided solid supporting evidence to adequately address my questions. They have earned my full endorsement on the acceptance of this paper." CBFF stated, "I am likely to increase the evaluation," and VLZy commented, "my problem was solved so I decided to raise my score." 

The key updates include:

**Benchmark Enhancements**: We added 152 multi-panel infographics with 780 expert-crafted co-referential questions to increase chart complexity (oq9S) and 54,376 non-template questions to increase linguistic diversity (oq9S, vLZy, and CBFF). We also retained and manually annotated “hard-parse” charts (oq9S) to improve the accuracy of QAs.

**Ethical Concerns**: To address ethical concerns (oq9S, XHUk, and CBFF), we clarified that we have IRB approval and will replace all images with URLs post-rebuttal, ensuring compliance with platform terms for non-commercial academic use. 

**Additional Experiments**: We conducted tests on non-template and co-referential questions, barebone infographics, and fine-grained question types (oq9S, Vcyr), demonstrating increased QA difficulty. We also validated the effectiveness of our benchmark in enhancing MLLMs performance via fine-tuninf (oq9S) and prompt optimization (vLZy).

**Clarifications**: We detailed data processing methods (vLZy), metaphor ambiguity handling (vLZy), and the rationale for visual cue removal in plain charts (Vcyr). We also clarified the minimal impact of parsing errors (CBFF) and provided evaluation instruction templates (vLZy).

We thank the reviewers again for the insightful comments, which have been valuable and helpful for us to improve our work. We also would like to express our deep gratitude to the AC and SAC for the effort in organizing the reviews.

Best regards,

The authors of #553

I thank the authors for their feedback and the complementary work they conducted for the rebuttal. I also appreciate the form of the response with a copy of the question (fixing my typo, thanks!) that facilitate the reading 

Q1/A1: errors seems thus quite marginal. I nevertheless encourage the author to report the results with a precision in accordance with the uncertainty of data

Q2/A2: reporting these statistics will be useful for a reader. If the place is missing in the main paper, it can be placed in the appendix.

Q3/A3: the fact the users are students (of the same age) with an expertise in machine learning biases the study. It is likely that their expectation differs from a more general population (in terms of age and, above all, expertise). From the answer and the protocol, it also seem that each QA was annotated by a unique user and assessed by two others. The fact that all 3 humans agree at 99.8% makes the study identical to an experiment where the "two humans" would have established the ground truth. Can it really be considered as a "user study"?  I think it worth to mention and discuss this point in the "limitation" section. 

Q4/A4 and Q5/A5: ok, thank you for the feedback. For A5, it could be added in the discussion.

Q6/A6: this experiment is interesting, it should be added (at least in the appendix)

Q7/A7: in the same vein, this information should be included in the paper (or appendix)

Again, I thank the author for their feedback. As a reviewer, spending lot of time to evaluate papers, it is enjoyable to read a serious and valuable piece of work. I am likely to increase the evaluation (expecting a serious discussion on the limitation of the user study will be included in the paper or the appendix).

Thank you for your follow-up comment regarding Q3.
We apologize for the confusion. The instruction in **A3** (*aggregation-00401-2*: *"How many bars are there?"*) is generated from a category-specific template: *"Your response should only contain the number of {placeholder} in the chart."* Here, the placeholder (e.g., "bar") is automatically filled based on the chart type. This means the instruction is not tailored to a specific image but is instead generated conditionally based on the data fact type and chart type.
All instructions are drawn from a predefined set of templates for different data fact types (see Table 2 in Appendix **A.3**). This strategy follows the recent practices such as CharXiv, and allows for better control over answer formats. Compared to using a single generic instruction for all questions, this approach improves consistency and supports more reliable evaluation of answer accuracy.

Dear Reviewers, ACs and SACs,

Thank you for all the inightful, constructive and positive feedback. We are encouraged by the recognition of the thoughtful construction of the benchmark, the scale and richness of the data, and the comprehensive evaluation and insightful analysis. Overall, there is general agreement on the following strengths:

**The thoughtful construction of benchmark**: All the reviewers agreed on the thoughtful construction of benchmark, **especially the paired infographic charts and plain charts**.
- R_oq9S: "By pairing identical data in plain vs. adorned form, the benchmark neatly isolates failures caused by visual clutter rather than underlying data complexity."
- R_oq9S: "(The authors) propose visual-element questions where the basic and metaphor subsets force models to ground icons and interpret pictorial metaphors, which most benchmarks fail to consider."
- R_Vcyr: "The authors present a rigorous methodology for constructing a high-quality and comprehensive dataset..."
- R_CBFF: "Providing pairs of infographics and corresponding plain chart is novel and can contribute to precisely estimate the part of the understanding difficulties (for VLM)..."
- R_vLZy: "Unlike most other benchmarks, this one includes questions specifically targeting visual elements, addressing the gap in benchmarks' ability to capture chart-specific designs."

**Scale and richness of the data**: All the reviewers agreed on the scales and richness of our benchmark compared to the existing benchmarks.
- R_oq9S: "It supports 54 types and >62 k QAs significantly exceed prior infographic datasets (InfographicVQA ≈5k charts, 1.1k visual QAs)..."
- R_CBFF: "The proposed benchmark is either richer or larger than most of previous benchmarks dealing with charts, in terms of number/type of questions."
- R_vLZy: "The data is sourced from real-world platforms..."

**Comprehensive evaluation and insightful analysis**: All the reviewers found our evaluation is comprehensive and valuable.
- R_oq9S: "The evaluation procedure is quite comprehensive...with element-removal and label-shuffle ablations."
- R_CBFF: "The evaluation is conducted over 20 models...Comparing such a large number of models for the considered task is insighful..."
- R_Vcyr: "The findings are clearly articulated and offer valuable insights into a problem that has seemingly been flying under the radar..."
- R_CBFF: "The analysis of section (4.2 and) 4.3 are interesting, identifying specific aspects that have an influence on the performance of the VLMs."

We are also deeply grateful for the reviewers' constructive feedback. We have carefully addressed their concerns, with main points summarized as follows:

**Clarifications**: 
- The detail on human involvement, including annotation of hard-parse charts, validation of auto-parse portion, and human evaluation (R_oq9S, R_CBFF).
- The justification and order of removing the visual cues (R_Vcyr, R_CBFF).
- The specific instructions and data processing (R_vLZy).
- The quantity and ambiguity of metaphor (R_oq9S, R_vLZy).

**Enhancement of benchmark**: 
- Provided the multi-panel infographics to increase chart complexity (R_oq9S).
- Provided expert-created non-template questions and co-referential questions to increase linguistic diversity (R_oq9S, R_vLZy).
- Modified the data including adding metadata on difficulty, removing charts without number, and replacing images with URLs (R_oq9S).


**Additional results**:
- Performed additional test on non-template and co-referential questions, fine-grained question types and barebone infographics (R_oq9S, R_Vcyr).
- Reported statistics on size, diversity and correlation between textual and visual performance (R_CBFF).
- Reported preliminary results on fine-tuning and prompt optimization (R_oq9S, R_vLZy).

We hope these responses can answer reviewers' questions. Finally, we would like to express our deep gratitude to the Area Chair for the amazing effort in organizing the reviews.

---

**Q1**: Data Privacy, Copyright, and Consent: The  most significant issue  involves collecting 5,642 infographic charts from 11 commercial platforms (Pinterest, Visual Capitalist, Statista, Behance, iStock) without clear  copyright permissions or  proper attribution. The supplementary material lists licenses  as "Custom" or "Not Applicable", which is inadequate.  Some platforms like  Pinterest and iStock likely have restrictive terms  that prohibit this  type of collection  and redistribution.

**A1**: Thank you for pointing out this issue. Reviewer oq9S (**A8**) also pointed out this and suggested the alternative distribution method of URLs. We will follow Reviewer oq9S's and your advice to change the distribution method by removing all the original images and replacing them with URLs. As updating data is prohibited during the rebuttal period, we will make these changes as soon as the rebuttal ends.

---

**Q2**: Improper Research  Involving Human Subjects:  While the human  involvement is minimal (expert consultation), the paper  lacks discussion of  selection criteria, or  ethical approval procedures. However, this is nlow risk given  the professional nature  of expert consultation.

**A2**: Thank you for pointing this out. We apologize for the unclear detail about human involvement. We will clarify this in camera-ready version, addressing your concerns as follows:
- **Selection Criteria**: All the experts were selected by two criteria: 1) They must have more than two years of research experience in visualization; 2) They must have published academic papers on top visualization venues such as VIS/TVCG. 
- **Ethical Approval**: We have obtained the IRB approval from our institution for human subject involvement. The approval number is THU-03-2025-1001. We have also explicitly asked for and obtained the experts' approval to distribute their annotations for academic purposes. 

**Q3**: Safety and Security: Potential violation  of platform terms  of service during  data collection, though this  appears to be  for legitimate academic purposes.

**A3**: Thank you for pointing this out. We carefully checked through all the platforms for terms of service:
- Most platforms explicitly state that they allow downloading the images for non-commercial use (Pinterest, Visual Capitalist, Statistica,  iStock, information is beautiful, designweek, Dataviz project).
- Other platforms (Behance, PNGEgg, marketing-partners, Cool infographics) attribute the ownership or copyright definition to the source links or the uploaders, without explicit terms of service prohibiting the collection.

To summarize, none of the platforms have terms banning the collection of data for our non-commercial academic purpose. In addition, the data were collected by humans without the risks of breaking rules against crawlers. To further mitigate the risk, we will replace all images with their URLs as we describe in **A1**.

## Response to Reviewer vLZy
We sincerely thank Reviewer vLZy for the thorough review and valuable feedback. We have addressed each point in our response below.

---

**Q1**: Based on the fact that text questions are still generated by templates, the diversity of questions is limited.

**A1**: Thank you. We have increased linguistic diversity with expert-written non-template questions. Please refer to **A2** for Reviewer oq9S for more details.

---

**Q2**: The paper analyzes the possible causes of performance degradation and does not propose targeted optimization methods.

**A2**: The analysis results of the causes of performance degradation can be used to improve model performance. For example, in Sec. 4.3.1, we found that the design-driven visual elements primarily contributed to the infographic chart degradation. Therefore, we revised the prompt instruction to explicitly guide the model to focus on visualization components rather than decorative elements:

*Instruction prompting:* *"Hint: Please be aware that this is an infographic chart. To obtain a more accurate answer, do not be influenced by its decorative elements; ignore such elements and focus your attention on the data visualization components."*

Due to time constraints, we only conducted this experiment on **GPT-4.1** with **20% of the dataset**. The results below show that performance improves when such instruction is added.

| Model    | Vanilla prompting | Instruction prompting |
|----------|-------------------|------------------------|
| GPT‑4.1  | 70.97             | 73.9                   |

---

**Q3**: I want to know how the specific instructions fed to certain models are constructed. In other words, if I want to reproduce the evaluation metrics of Qwen2.5VL and GPT‑4o on this dataset, how should I construct the complete instruction input to the models based on the given questions?  

**A3**: Thanks for pointing this out. We will add the complete instruction input in the supplemental material. The input format of our questions is to place the **instruction after the question**, as: `f"{question} \n {instruction}"`. For example, in *aggregation‑00401‑2*, the question is: *"How many bars are there?"* and the instruction is:  *"\* Your response should only contain the number of bars in the chart."* The final input would be: *"How many bars are there? \* Your response should only contain the number of bars in the chart."*

---

**Q4**: Additionally, the data processing methods used during evaluation should be mentioned in the paper—for example, handling of letter casing (uppercase/lowercase), modifications of special symbols, etc.

**A4**: For text answers, we:  
- convert all characters to lowercase,  
- standardize special symbols (e.g., replacing single quotes with double quotes),  
- remove leading, trailing, and consecutive whitespace characters.  

For numerical answers, we:  
- extract the numerical part,  
- remove their units (e.g., “$”),  
- convert them into a unified numerical format to facilitate direct numerical comparison.  

As mentioned in Sec. 4.1, different metrics are then applied for text and numeric answers.

---

**Q5**: Under the issue of metaphor, some universal icons like national flags have the same meaning across different cultural systems. However, for certain animals such as snakes, their symbolic meanings may vary in different cultural contexts. So how should such issues be addressed?

**A5**: This concern was carefully considered during the question design phase. To minimize potential ambiguity, we deliberately avoided using metaphorical elements or icons that could be interpreted differently across cultures. Furthermore, we invited experts from diverse cultural backgrounds—including China, the United States, Hong Kong, and the United Kingdom—to review and verify the questions. This ensures that all questions are culturally neutral and free from ambiguous or culturally sensitive interpretations.

## Response to Reviewer CBFF
We sincerely thank Reviewer CBFF for the thorough review and valuable feedback. We have addressed each point in our response below.

---

**Q1**: In the chart-to-translation step, it is not clear which proportion of the dataset is validated automatically, that is when both Gemini 2.0 Flash and GPT‑4o agree on the extracted data (consensus). 5% of error is still quite high and it thus does not make sense to report numbers with precision in Table 2 with such imprecision.

**A1**: Among the 2,719 charts where Gemini 2.0 Flash and GPT‑4o reached consensus, fewer than 5% contained errors. Most of the errors occur only on a few data points in the table. To assess the impact of these errors, we manually examined the errors along with the associated questions and found that only 0.2% of the questions are affected, indicating a minimal impact on the reported results. We will conduct a thorough manual review of all questions to further ensure the dataset’s reliability.

---

**Q2**: The number of charts considered (5,642) is significantly smaller than previous published benchmarks. It may be relevant to report the richness of the vocabulary of the questions or their diversity (e.g., with the average cosine similarity between all questions). In the proposed work, the text-based questions are generated from a template and thus are likely to be less diverse in their expression than, e.g., the crowd-sourced questions of [7] or the human-generated questions of OpenCQA and ChartQA.

**A2**: Thanks for pointing this out. We include the number of charts, the richness of the vocabulary, and their diversity in Table 4, shown below. The richness of the vocabulary is measured by the **Hypergeometric Distribution (HD-D)** score [1], which estimates lexical diversity based on the probability of unique word types in random samples. The diversity is measured by the **Semantic Diversity** score [2], which quantifies variability in semantic content via average pairwise embedding distance and is also used in ChartQAPro. 

As we can see, the HD-D score of our dataset is **0.812**, notably higher than ChartBench (**0.6302**) and comparable to high-quality datasets like ChartQAPro and InfographicVQA. It indicates that our dataset has a rich and evenly distributed vocabulary. The Semantic Diversity score of our dataset is also comparable to ChartQAPro, indicating broad semantic coverage with balanced question types and expressions.

| Dataset          | Charts  | Questions | HD-D   | Semantic Diversity |
|------------------|---------|-----------|--------|--------------------|
| ChartQA          | 1.6K    | 2.5K      | 0.769  | 0.805              |
| ChartBench       | 2.1K    | 16.8K     | 0.630  | 0.743              |
| InfographicVQA   | 5.4K    | 30.0K     | 0.828  | 0.864              |
| ChartQAPro       | 1.3K    | 1.9K      | **0.837** | **0.823**         |
| **InfoChartQA**  | **11.6K** | **56.0K** | 0.812  | 0.800              |

[1] Yuan-Quan Wang, Ying-Ying Zhang, and Jia-Lei Liu. Expectation identity of the hypergeometric distribution and its application in the calculations of high-order origin moments. *Communications in Statistics-Theory and Methods* 52.17 (2023): 6018-6036.  
[2] Ahmed Masry, Mohammed Saidul Islam, et al. *ChartQAPro: A more diverse and challenging benchmark for chart question answering*. arXiv preprint arXiv:2504.05506, 2025.

---

**Q3**: The human evaluation is not enough documented: how many persons were included in the study? What is their background w.r.t. machine learning and data visualization? Are they authors of the paper? What is the repartition in terms of country, mother tongue, age, gender? More importantly, to which extent do they agree between them? Why do they have a 4–5% error in comparison to the ground truth? It also raises the question of the inter-annotator agreement when the benchmark ground truth is made.

**A3**: Our human evaluation involved **15 participants**, including **14 males and 1 female**, all of whom are **native Chinese speakers**. They were **graduate students (aged 20–30)** from universities in China, with expertise in **deep learning and visualization**. None of the participants are authors of this paper. 

To ensure the accuracy of the ground truth annotations, at least **two humans reviewed all manually provided QAs**, preventing potential inaccuracies caused by individuals. For auto-generated QAs, as noted in **A1**, the accuracy of the extracted tables is **99.8%**, ensuring the accuracy of the QAs.

---

**Q4**: Licence of Qwen2.5-VL-72B/Adding 'accuracy' in Table 2.

**A4**: Thank you for pointing it out. We will revise it and thoroughly review the paper to fix similar issues.

---

**Q5**: Beyond the number of visual elements (Section 4.3), it could be interesting to characterize the 'creative visual elements' in the infographics. Are there some 'types' of visual elements that are likely to favor/be detrimental to the VLM understanding? However, Section 4.3.2 partially addresses this aspect, by identifying the importance of "connections".

**A5**: According to our experiments in Sec. 4.3.1, such creative visual elements are detrimental to MLLM understanding. As we can see, when the creative visual elements are removed gradually (e.g., from Fig. 3(a) to Fig. 3(e)), the model performance decreases accordingly. This validates that the creative visual elements are the primary cause of the performance drop on infographic charts.

---

**Q6**: It is not clear how the order of removing is determined. Does the performance drop change when this order is modified? If yes, to which extent (standard deviation on the curves of Fig. 4)?

**A6**: In this experiment, we aimed to remove the more important elements first to better assess their impact. To achieve this, elements were removed **in descending order of size**, as larger elements are generally intended to convey more important or prominent information. We also **randomly shuffled the order of removal**. The results below show that both removal strategies exhibit similar performance degradation trends, indicating that the order of removal has **little impact on the overall performance drop**.

| Removal order / # of visual elements | 0     | 5     | 10    | 15    | 20    | 25    | 30    | 35    | 40    |
|--------------------------------------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| By Size                              | 87.65 | 82.71 | 80.34 | 79.42 | 79.47 | 79.21 | 79.06 | 78.89 | 76.90 |
| Random                               | 87.65 | 82.09 | 80.38 | 79.41 | 78.38 | 79.07 | 79.70 | 78.04 | 76.90 |

---

**Q7**: It could be relevant to quantitatively estimate the correlation between the performance in text-based questions and those that are visual-based (Section 4.2).

**A7**: The **Spearman correlation coefficient** between performance on text-based and visual-based questions is **0.9376** (*p* < 0.01). This suggests that models performing well on text-based questions tend to also perform well on visual-based questions, highlighting the **consistency and generalizability** of our benchmark for evaluating MLLMs.

## Response to Reviewer oq9S

We sincerely thank Reviewer oq9S for the thorough review and valuable feedback. We have addressed each point in our response below.

**Q1:** Manually select authentic multi-panel infographics with rich inter-panel links.

**A1:** We manually added 152 authentic multi-panel infographics with inter-panel links.Although such multi-panel infographic charts account for only a small portion of the benchmark (2.7%), we believe this is reasonable, as such infographic charts are rare in the real world.Since the underlying data of these multi-panel infographic charts is complex, automatically generated questions tend to be inaccurate, especially the co-referential ones that require linking entities in different panels to answer. Therefore, for these infographic charts, we invited four visualization experts to designed 780 complex co-referential questions.

---
**Q2:** Crowd-source or expert-write non-templated, co-referential questions for the test split.

**A2:** We invited visualization experts to enhance the questions as detailed below.

- **Non-template**: We semi-automatically created the non-template questions. The experts manually rewrote **1,376 general non-template questions** on **405 infographic samples** that covered all the chart types and data facts in the original dataset. Next, we used Gemini-2.5-Flash and GPT-4o to expand the non-template set by paraphrasing all the other existing template questions. The models are prompted to mimic the natural expression and diversity of the expert-written questions, producing **54,376 non-template questions** to replace the original template ones.

- **Co-referential**: For the multi-panel infographic charts, the experts designed **780 complex co-referential questions**. Please refer to **A1** for more details.

We conducted additional experiments on the non-template questions, as shown in the table below. Specifically, we selected three proprietary MLLMs used in our original experiments. Compared to the overall results in the original experiments (template), the non-template diversity indeed increases the difficulty and causes a drop in overall accuracy. We also tested the models on the special co-referential questions, with results shown in the “Multiple” column of the table below. It shows that the accuracy on co-referential questions drops significantly, indicating that these questions are particularly challenging for MLLMs.


| Model                    | Overall (template) | Overall (non-template) | Multiple |
|--------------------------|-------------------:|-----------------------:|---------:|
| OpenAI O4-mini           | 79.41             | 76.23                 | 31.58    |
| GPT-4o                   | 66.09             | 64.59                 | 28.97    |
| Gemini 2.5 Pro Preview   | 83.31             | 79.23                 | 36.45    |
---

**Q3**: Optionally auto-generate a training split and demonstrate that light finetuning (LoRA, Q-LoRA) yields measurable gains, validating the usefulness of the synthetic portion.

**A3**: We randomly selected 30k questions from the synthetic portion as the training set and used the remaining questions as the test set. The training set was then used to fine-tune the LLaVA One Vision 7B model with LoRA. The experimental results show that its performance on text-based questions improved from the original **38.41%** to **50.19%** on the test set, which demonstrates the usefulness of the synthetic portion.

---

**Q4**: Keep the “hard-parse” charts (those that today’s MLLMs cannot table-ize) and provide gold tables, so future systems can attack the full end-to-end problem rather than an already-solved sub-task.

**A4**: We would like to clarify that we did not discard the "hard-parse" charts. As described in the second paragraph in Sec. 3.2, the charts where the models disagreed, which are considered as hard charts for MLLMs, were preserved. Their gold tables were annotated by human experts to ensure the difficulty of the benchmark. We will revise this paragraph to clarify this.

---

**Q5**: Creating questions with a template per diagram/graph type introduces biases. 55k text questions come from a fixed library of templates tied to 11 “data-fact” types, limiting linguistic diversity and probably favoring LLMs pre-exposed to similar wording.

**A5**:Thank you. We increase linguistic diversity with expert-written non-template questions. Please refer to **A2** for more details. More statistics about the diversity can be found in **A2** for Reviewer CBFF.

---

**A6**: Please refer to **A4** for more details.

---

**A7**: To supplement the metadata on per-chart difficulty, we define the difficulty level of a chart based on the performance of GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Pro on it.
Specifically, a chart is classified as:
- **"Easy"** if the average accuracy exceeds 80%.
- **"Moderate"** if the average accuracy ranges from 40% to 80%.
- **"Difficult"** if the average accuracy of the two models on it is below 40%.

The table below shows additional experimental results on subsets of different difficulties. We will include this information in the metadata, including the difficulty levels and the specific accuracy score for each chart.

|                  | Easy | Moderate | Hard  |
|------------------|--------|----------|-------|
| OpenAI O4-mini   | 85.68  | 63.45    | 29.00 |
| GPT-4o           | 74.27  | 48.35    | 24.41 |
| Gemini 2.5 Pro Preview | 87.53  | 69.34    | 32.75 |

---

---

**A9**: We would like to explain that metaphor is a phenomenon rare in quantity but significant for conveying intricate narratives in infographics. It also requires intensive labor from experts to manually identify the metaphor and design subtle metaphor-related questions. Therefore, although the size of our metaphor set is smaller, it reflects the distribution of metaphors in the real world, and the sophisticated human annotations make the small set still valuable. In addition, compared to other purely human-annotated plain chart datasets such as CharXiv and ChartQAPro with about 1,000–2,000 charts, the metaphor set we provided is a non-negligible addition for a special category.

---

**A10**: Thank you for pointing it out. We will revise it.

---

**A11**: Thank you. We have checked through the dataset and removed the images without numbers. We have also used non-template questions to replace awkward template ones as detailed in **A2**.

summary.value: The paper introduces InfoChartQA, a new benchmark that pairs 5642 real‐world infographic charts with automatically rendered plain versions covering 54 fine-grained chart types. The authors provide 55091 text-based questions generated from 40-odd data-fact templates and 7475 visual-element questions (7k basic + 462 metaphor) crafted by experts. A chart-to-table step ensembles GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash, keeping only charts the two models parse identically (>95% spot accuracy) and manually annotating the rest. Twenty MLLMs, plus human annotators, are benchmarked; proprietary Gemini-2.5 Pro tops the leaderboard (almost reaching human performances) but still shows a ≈10% drop from plain to infographic charts. Ablation studies reveal performance falls as the number of design-driven visual elements rises.

strengths_contributions.value:
The paper is well written and easy to follow. The whole dataset creation and pipeline is well explained. 
By pairing identical data in plain vs. adorned form, the benchmark neatly isolates failures caused by visual clutter rather than underlying data complexity. It supports 54 types and >62 k QAs significantly exceed prior infographic datasets (InfographicVQA ≈5k charts, 1.1k visual QAs) and propose visual-element questions where the basic and metaphor subsets force models to ground icons and interpret pictorial metaphors, which most benchmarks fail to consider. Moreover, the evaluation procedure is quite comprehensive of multiple proprietary and open models wirh  20 diverse MLLMs + human baseline, with element-removal and label-shuffle ablations.

ethical_considerations.value: Yes, there are ethics concerns that require attention by the authors

ethical_comments.value: I recommend the authors either (i) obtain explicit permissions / release only URLs, or (ii) strip the images and distribute annotations plus download scripts so users fetch the charts directly, as done by WebVid and LAION.

dataset_code_comments.value: While going through the dataset, I noticed some of the charts don't show numbers but the question expect a number as answer, which humans also have difficulty at doing it. And the questions (using the template) might be very awkward. Look at split "info", question_id "extreme-01441-2" example: `What is the minimum value of value of green?` where the answer should be 18 but no lines indicate the number 18, which makes it guessing and the template question is not natural.

final_justification.value: Strong idea and careful initial benchmark design; the authors responded admirably and the updated artifact appears much stronger. However, **the post-rebuttal additions (large-scale non-template and co-referential questions, multi-panel set, new ablations) materially change the paper relative to what was submitted**, and the new results are not yet comprehensively vetted. For process integrity and reproducibility, I recommend Reject (encourage resubmission) so the improved dataset and analyses can undergo a full review cycle in other top conferences or journals. I would be positive on a resubmission centered on the updated benchmark and complete evaluations.

summary.value: This paper presents **InfoChartQA**, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate MLLMs on infographic understanding. The benchmark comprises 5.6K pairs of infographic and corresponding plain charts generated from the same underlying data. The results show that even the top-performing MLLMs suffer great accuracy drops in understanding the artifact-rich infographics. This paper also shows that MLLMs have great difficulties understanding metaphorical meanings behind visual elements in infographics.

strengths_contributions.value: This is a well-executed and thoughtfully motivated piece of work. The authors present a rigorous methodology for constructing a high-quality and comprehensive dataset, addressing an important challenge in infographic understanding. The findings are clearly articulated and offer valuable insights into a problem that has seemingly been flying under the radar in existing benchmarks, despite its practical significance.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
While the paper presents strong and thorough contributions, I still have a few *relatively minor* concerns—primarily related to ensuring **the** **fairness of this benchmark's evaluations**:

* **Visual Fidelity in Plain Chart Counterparts**: Since the plain chart counterparts are reconstructed from extracted tabular data, some meaningful visual cues may be lost during the re-rendering process, potentially introducing unintended disparities. For instance, as noted in Appendix B.2.1 (Page 20), distinct 'pencil colors' used in the original chart are lost, resulting in single-colored bars. This raises the question: can the loss of such visual distinctions greatly affect models' performances that suggest unfair “apples-to-oranges” evaluations?  
* **Need for an Intermediate ‘Barebone Infographic’ Baseline**: It may be helpful to include results on a transitional category of infographic charts — what I would call *“Barebone Infographic”* — that retain core visual structures but remove decorative or obstructive visual artifacts (e.g., as shown in Figure 3(e)). Although the authors do perform some ablation studies along these lines, the experiments are limited to only GPT-4.1 and TinyChart. Including more models in the benchmark table with a full spectrum — from Original Infographic, Barebone Infograpic, to Plain Chart — may offer a fuller understanding of how various visual features impact performance in a more fine-grained fashion.  
* **Evaluation Category Granularity**: The authors mention following PlotQA’s evaluation setup, but the current presentation mixes question types (e.g., free-form numeric vs. multiple-choice). It would improve clarity and fairness if the results were reported in separate question-type categories, enabling more granular comparisons of model capabilities over individual answer formats.

final_justification.value: The authors have adequately addressed my minor concerns by further fulfilling some of the potential flaws that I pointed out. Given that I did not find any major error in the first place, I am convinced that this work is worth being accepted.

summary.value:
The work deals with 'infographic charts' that differ from classical 'plain charts' in the sense they integrate various creative visual elements to ease the understanding of complex ideas. It fisrt consist to create a dataset of 5,642 'infographic charts', colelcted from several websites (Pinterest, Visual Capitalist, Statista, Behance and iStock) and classified in 54 types (at least 30charts per type). The process implied both manual work with experts of students and the use of a VLM. The corresponding raw data were then extracted with two VLMs. A manual verification of 500 charts showed that 95% of those where both VLM agree are correct, thus all the data in such a case were considered. The other were manually annotated. A set of 55k text-based question is created from a template that is adapted to the type of data fact available in the charts. Moreover, they created a set of 7k questions related to visual elements in the charts, including a small number (154) of questions related to the metaphoric sense conveyed by the infographics. 

Then, 20 VLM were evaluated on the proposed dataset, including 14 models that are open-source. It has also be tested by humans on a subset (10%) of the benchmark. It shows a significant drop in performance for the infographic chart in comparison to their plain counterpart, while it is not the case for humans. Further analysis are conducted to identify which element have an influence on the performance.

strengths_contributions.value:
* infographics is a very common material on the Web and media and is thus of interest to estimate the ability of VLM to understand them. To my knowledge, providing pairs of infographics and corresponding plain chart is novel and can contribute to precisely estimate the part of the understanding difficulties (for VLM) that is due to the additive creative visual elements that are specific to the infographics.

* beyond the specific aspect of dealing with infographic charts, the proposed benchmark is either richer or larger than most of previous benchmarks dealing with charts, in terms of number/type of questions (see Table 1).

* the evaluation is conducted over 20 models, including 6 proprietary one and 14 that are in open-access (at least) for academic research. Comparing such a large number of models for the considered task is insighfull. In particular, some models are tested in various size/version and it thus allows to directly compare their performance (although this aspect is not particularly highlighted in the paper).

* the analysis of section (4.2 and) 4.3 are interesting, identifying specific aspects that have an influence on the performance of the VLMs.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
* In the chart-to-translation step, it is not clear which proportion of the dataset is validated automatically, that is when both Gemini 2.0 flash and GPT-4o agree on the extracted data (concensus). 5% or error is still quite high and it thus does not make sense to report numbers with $1e-4$ precision in Table 2 with such imprecision.

* The number of charts considered (5642) is significantly smaller than previous published benchmarks. In Table 1, it would be fairer to report the number of chart for each of them (e.g 20k for ChartQA) and include all those cited in section 2 (100k charts for FigureQA, 7k questions for DVQA...). It may be relevant to report the richness of the vocabulary of the question or their diversity (e.g with the average cosine similarity between all questions). In the proposed work, the text-based question are generated from a template thus are likely to be less diverse in their expression than e.g the crowd-sourced questions of [7] or the human -generated questions of OpenCQA and ChartQA. However, it is not obsious and would thus be of interest to be studied.

* the human evaluation is not enough documented: how many persons were included in the study? what is their background w.r.t machine learning and data vizaulization? Are they author of the paper? What is the repartitionin terms of (working/living) country, mother tongue, age, (gender) ? More importantly, to which extent do they agree between them ? Why do they have a 4-5% error in comparison to the ground truth (is it related to the "5% error" mentioned above) ? 
  - It also raise the question of the inter-annotator agreement when the benchmark ground thruth is made.

ethical_considerations.value: Yes, there are ethics concerns that require attention by the authors

ethical_comments.value:
The data that are considered may relate to humans but are not sensitive since they usually agregate data from many persons. Actually, they are data that can be commonly found in media.

It is nevertheless not clear whether the licence of the data used to build the benchmark allowed their usage and redistribution in such a context. Nothing is reported in the paper regardin gthis aspect, or any filtering taht would have been applied according to th elicence of the original data. Question 12 of the Check List refers to Section C of the supplementary material that lists the "Licences for Data". However, it only reports "Custom" or "Not Applicable" that is rather vague. By going directly to the site mentioned, it seems there is no problem for some of them (e.g Statista) but it is less clear for others (e.g Pinterest, iStock...)

dataset_code_comments.value:
Both dataset and code are available. The code is extensively commented with examples to conduct the evaluation easily, with step-by-step instructions. 

The Dataset Card is also well documented.

additional_feedback.value:
* in appendix C2, the licence of Qwen2.5-VL-72B is rather "custom" than "proprietary". Actually, [the licence](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct/blob/main/LICENSE) allows to reuse, modify (...) the model (section 2 and 3), except for product and service with more than 100M monthly user (section 4), thus allows to use it for research.
* in Table 2, it should be explicit that the number represent an accuracy (classification rate).
* beyond the number of visual elements (section 4.3) it could be interesting to characterize the 'creative visual elements' in the infographics. Are there some 'types' of visual elements that are likely to favour/be detrimental to the VLM understanding? However, section 4.3.2 partially addresses this aspect, by identifying the importance of "connetions".
* it is not clear how the order of removing is determined? Does the performance drop change when this order is modified? If yes, to which extent (standard deviation on the curves of Fig. 4)?
* it could be relevant to quantitavely estimate the correlation between the performance in text-based questions and those that are visual-based (section4.2)

final_justification.value: The rebuttal was constructive and addressed most of my concerns. I am confident that the author will include the proposed changes in the final version and I thus propose to accept the paper

summary.value:
The paper presents InfoChartQA, a novel benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on infographic chart understanding. 

- Background and Motivation: Infographic charts, which integrate design - driven visual elements like pictograms and icons with standard chart types, pose challenges to MLLMs due to the need for both visual recognition and reasoning. 
- Existing visual question - answering benchmarks fall short in assessing these capabilities of MLLMs as they lack paired plain charts and visual - element - based questions.
- Benchmark Construction: InfoChartQA consists of 5,642 pairs of infographic and plain charts sharing the same underlying data but differing in visual presentations. It also includes visual - element - based questions to capture the unique visual designs and communicative intent of infographic charts. The construction process involves infographic chart dataset construction, paired infographic and plain chart generation, and multimodal question and answer construction.
- Key Findings: Evaluation of 20 MLLMs reveals a substantial performance decline on infographic charts, particularly for visual - element - based questions related to metaphors. Thepaired charts enable fine - grained error analysis and ablation studies, which show that factors like the proximity between icons and data values, visual complexity, and text label orders impact model performance.
- Contributions: The paper presents the first benchmark with paired infographic and plain charts, introduces a rich set of visual - element - based QAs for infographic charts, and identifies and analyzes the performance gap of current MLLMs in interpreting infographic charts versus plain charts.

In conclusion, InfoChartQA provides a new perspective and a reliable foundation for evaluating and advancing MLLMs in infographic chart question answering.

This helps determine whether errors stem from the complexity of the data itself or from the additional visual elements used in the infographic.

- The data is sourced from real-world platforms, and the screening process employs Gemini and a semi-automated workflow, ensuring high efficiency.

- Based on the fact that text questions are still generated by templates, the diversity of questions is limited.

title.value: InfoChartQA: A Benchmark for Multimodal Question Answering on Infographic Charts

TLDR.value: We build InfoChartQA, a benchmark for multimodal question answering on infographic charts.

abstract.value: Understanding infographic charts with design-driven visual elements (e.g., pictograms, icons) requires both visual recognition and reasoning, posing challenges for multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing visual question answering benchmarks fall short in evaluating these capabilities of MLLMs due to the lack of paired plain charts and visual-element-based questions. To bridge this gap, we introduce InfoChartQA, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on infographic chart understanding. It includes 5,642 pairs of infographic and plain charts, each sharing the same underlying data but differing in visual presentations. We further design visual-element-based questions to capture their unique visual designs and communicative intent. Evaluation of 20 MLLMs reveals a substantial performance decline on infographic charts, particularly for visual-element-based questions related to metaphors. The paired infographic and plain charts enable fine-grained error analysis and ablation studies, which highlight new opportunities for advancing MLLMs in infographic chart understanding. We release InfoChartQA at https://github.com/CoolDawnAnt/InfoChartQA.
